slides: Okay, a quick summary before the practice.
Everything important about averages, in about three minutes.
Symmetric numbers? Then the average is the middle. No calculation.
And evenly spaced numbers are symmetric too. So it's the middle one, or first plus last, over two.
And the average always sits between the smallest and the largest value.
Now, the most useful move is to turn it around. Sum equals number times average.
You don't know the values? Well, you don't need them. Treat every value as the average.
A value joins or leaves? Change the sum, and change what you divide by.
The differences from the average always add up to zero.
Plus eight too many above. So the missing one is eight below. Seventy-two.
Numbers near a round number? Work only with the differences.
One value changes? Share the change over all the values.
Every value changes the same way? Then the average changes the same way.
And both at once? Same order. Times two, then plus five.
Five ones? Only if they're allowed to be equal. Different integers? One, two, three, four, five.
Compare the new value to the new average. Then share that extra among the old values.
And check, is it before the new value joined, or after?
On the exam it just says "average". So you have to notice the weights yourself.
Each value times its weight. Then divide by the sum of the weights... not by the number of values.
The distances are just the weights, flipped.
Thirty and ninety. That's a gap of sixty, so five parts of twelve. One part from the heavy side... forty-two.
Only two kinds of items? Start everyone at the low value. Then share the extra.
Combining groups? The size of each group is its weight.
And before you calculate... the answer is on the side of the bigger group.
So, before you practice, ask yourself these questions.
And the traps: taking the average of two group averages when the groups aren't equal, dividing by the wrong number, and counting before instead of after.
Good luck.
